challenges.name: Dig Streak
challenges.note: Nine correct actions in a row

hazards.coupler-release: That is the coupler's manual release, not its lock indicator. Pressing it before the pins are confirmed engaged is exactly how a bucket lets go of the stick mid-swing, with nothing underneath it but whoever happens to be in the way when it drops.
hazards.spoil-surcharge: That spoil is piled back onto the very edge you just cut. The extra surcharge weight sitting right at the crest is what turns a wall that would otherwise have held its own weight into one that lets go without any further warning at all.
hazards.swing-radius-stand: You are standing inside the excavator's swing radius while the house is rigged to slew. The counterweight sweeps that space at head height with no warning a person on foot can react to in time, which is why the radius has to be barricaded before the machine ever swings, not watched for by whoever happens to be standing nearby.
hazards.unverified-dig-zone: You are cutting into ground the locate ticket covers before the paint on it was actually checked against that ticket. A buried gas or electric line gives the bucket no warning before it is struck, and the operator finds out the same second everyone downstream of that line does.

interrupts.alert: A second crew member has walked up the blind side of the house to grab a tool, right where the counterweight sweeps.
interrupts.cue: Stop the cut and get the spotter to move them clear before the house swings again.
interrupts.missNote: The house swung through the blind quadrant with a coworker still standing in it. A slewing counterweight gives no warning of its own, and a person it strikes rarely gets a second chance.
interrupts.why: The cab's mirrors never fully cover the blind quadrant behind the counterweight, which is exactly why a spotter's whole job is watching ground the operator physically cannot see. Calling the spotter the instant someone appears in that quadrant is the only control that catches a person the seat itself cannot.
interrupts.wrongNote: Not that — the person in the blind quadrant is what has to be dealt with before this cut continues at all.

interrupts.alert: The stick has drifted closer to the marked utility line than the plan allows while attention was on the spoil side.
interrupts.cue: Signal stop now, before the bucket reaches the marked line.
interrupts.missNote: The bucket kept swinging toward the marked line while attention stayed on the spoil side. A struck utility line does not wait for the swing to finish before it lets go.
interrupts.why: A locate mark is painted within a tolerance around where the line is believed to run, not on its exact centreline, so the safe working distance is measured outward from that paint for as long as the bucket is moving — not only at the moment the cut started. A drift nobody calls out is a drift that keeps closing that distance unattended.
interrupts.wrongNote: Not that — the drift toward the marked line is what has to stop this swing right now.

lateNotes.grade-rod: The grade checker reads the rod against the plan invert while the cut is still open and easy to correct, not after the pipe is already laid to whatever depth the bucket happened to stop at.
lateNotes.vac-hose: The line gets hand- or vacuum-exposed before the bucket goes anywhere near it, not after the bucket has already found out where it is the hard way.

name: Excavator Trench & Utility Locate

passRule.note: stars >= 2 and no unsafe action (WebXR/shared/records.js passed())

steps.cue: Hi-vis vest and hard hat before anyone is near the machine.
steps.prompt: Hi-vis vest and hard hat before anyone is near the machine.
steps.title: Suit up before the swing radius
steps.why: The whole reason a spotter can catch a worker in the blind quadrant at all is that a hi-vis vest reads against dirt and steel from a cab several feet up — a spotter who cannot pick a person out of the background is watching the ground for nothing, and the hard hat is what a dropped tool or a low swing has something other than a skull to hit first.

steps.cue: Confirm which utilities the one-call ticket covers before anything on the ground is trusted.
steps.prompt: Confirm which utilities the one-call ticket covers before anything on the ground is trusted.
steps.title: Read the locate ticket
steps.why: The ticket is what tells you which lines were actually marked for this dig and which ones were not — a mark on the ground with no ticket behind it could be leftover paint from a different job, and a ticket with no mark on the ground yet means the utility owner has not located that line at all. Reading it first is what makes the paint mean something.

steps.cue: Walk the ground the ticket covers. Three marks here do not actually prove where a line is — find them by looking.

decoyNotes.verified-mark: That line is freshly painted, single colour, and matches the ticket. Nothing to flag there.

itemNames.unmarked-flag: flag with no paint behind it

itemNotes.conflicting-mark: Two different utility colours crossing at the same spot with no legend to explain it is a mark nobody should dig against until the locator is called back.
itemNotes.faded-mark: Paint this faded could be from a locate weeks old — it needs a fresh call before anyone trusts it over today's dig.
itemNotes.unmarked-flag: A flag standing with no paint line leading to it is an incomplete locate, not a located line — it tells you a utility is somewhere near, not where.

steps.prompt: Walk the ground the ticket covers. Three marks here do not actually prove where a line is — find them by looking.
steps.title: Verify the locate marks against the ticket
steps.why: A mark on the ground only means what a competent locate put there, and paint that is faded, contradictory or unfinished is not that — it is a line whose real position nobody has actually confirmed today. Digging against a mark like that trades the appearance of a located utility for the fact of one, and the bucket cannot tell the difference until it has already struck something.

steps.cue: Cone both approaches and set the barrier around the machine's full swing.
steps.prompt: Cone both approaches and set the barrier around the machine's full swing.
steps.title: Barricade the swing radius
steps.why: OSHA's equipment rule at 29 CFR 1926 Subpart O treats the swing radius as ground the employer has to control, not ground a pedestrian is expected to judge for themselves — a barrier that exists before the house ever slews is what keeps a shortcut across the yard from ending inside the counterweight's own path.

steps.cue: Trigger the alarm and commit only once it reads in the audible range over yard noise.

gauge.label: TRAVEL ALARM — SOUND LEVEL
gauge.missNote: Too quiet to carry over the yard. Get it serviced before this machine moves again.

steps.prompt: Trigger the alarm and commit only once it reads in the audible range over yard noise.
steps.title: Test the travel alarm
steps.why: A travel alarm nobody can hear over the yard's own noise is a travel alarm that has already failed the one job it has, which is why it gets tested against today's actual conditions before the first move, not assumed from the label on the horn.

steps.cue: Agree hand signals and the stop signal with the dedicated spotter before the first cut.
steps.prompt: Agree hand signals and the stop signal with the dedicated spotter before the first cut.
steps.title: Confirm the spotter's protocol
steps.why: The spotter is watching ground and blind quadrants the operator's own seat cannot see, and that only works if both of them already agree what a stop signal looks like before it is ever needed — sorting that out mid-swing is sorting it out too late.

steps.cue: Turn the coupler lever fully to the locked position before trusting the bucket.
steps.prompt: Turn the coupler lever fully to the locked position before trusting the bucket.
steps.title: Lock the quick coupler
steps.why: A quick coupler that is seated but not turned all the way to locked can still let go of the bucket under load — a confirmed, positive lock is the whole point of the mechanism, and the seating on its own is only the part that looks finished before it actually is.

steps.cue: Carry the vacuum hose to the marked line and expose it before the bucket comes anywhere close.

drag.missNote: Not over the marked line — line the hose up with the paint before you start exposing anything.

steps.prompt: Carry the vacuum hose to the marked line and expose it before the bucket comes anywhere close.
steps.title: Hand-expose the marked line
steps.why: The last foot or two of cover over a marked utility is exposed by hand or vacuum, never by the bucket, because a locate mark's tolerance is measured in feet and a bucket's teeth are not precise enough to stop at a line nobody can actually see yet. Exposing it first turns a guess about depth into a fact the operator can actually dig against.

steps.cue: Hold the controls steady for a slow, controlled pass now that the line is exposed.
steps.holdBreakNote: Released the controls mid-cut, next to an exposed line. Hold it through the whole pass — that is what keeps this a controlled cut instead of a guess.
steps.prompt: Hold the controls steady for a slow, controlled pass now that the line is exposed.
steps.title: Make the controlled cut
steps.why: A controlled pass next to an exposed line is slow on purpose — the bucket is close enough now that a fast, confident cut is exactly the moment a small misjudgement in depth or reach turns into a struck line the crew has to now report and repair on top of the job they came to do.

steps.cue: Keep the spotter's signal steady, holding the swing path clear of both the crew and the marked line.
steps.holdBreakNote: The swing path drifted out of the safe corridor. Bring the signal back on line before the bucket swings again.
steps.prompt: Keep the spotter's signal steady, holding the swing path clear of both the crew and the marked line.
steps.title: Direct the swing away from the line
steps.why: The swing path has two things it must stay clear of at once — the ground crew on one side and the marked utility on the other — and a spotter giving continuous signals is what keeps the operator's attention on both instead of narrowing down to whichever one is currently in view out the side glass.

steps.cue: Relocate the excavated soil at least two feet back from the cut.
steps.prompt: Relocate the excavated soil at least two feet back from the cut.
steps.title: Set the spoil back from the edge
steps.why: Spoil stacked at the crest adds surcharge load exactly where the wall is already under the most stress, and setting it back the two feet OSHA's excavation rule expects takes that extra weight out of the equation before it has a chance to matter.

steps.cue: Have the grade checker read the rod against the plan invert while the cut is still open.
steps.prompt: Have the grade checker read the rod against the plan invert while the cut is still open.
steps.title: Confirm the cut against the grade rod
steps.why: A second person reading the rod against the plan, independent of whoever is running the machine, is what actually catches a cut that is running shallow or deep before the pipe goes in on top of it — the operator's own sense of how deep the bucket went is not the same thing as a measurement.

steps.cue: Read the density gauge on the first backfill lift and commit only inside the target band.

gauge.label: BACKFILL LIFT DENSITY
gauge.missNote: Under target. Run the compactor over this lift again before the next one goes on.

steps.prompt: Read the density gauge on the first backfill lift and commit only inside the target band.
steps.title: Check the backfill lift density
steps.why: Backfill placed in lifts is only doing its job if each lift is actually compacted to the target density before the next one goes on top of it — a lift that reads soft now is a settlement problem under the surface months later, and the gauge is what tells you before that lift disappears under the next one.

steps.cue: Log the cut, the locate ticket number and the backfill sign-off before shutting the machine down.
steps.prompt: Log the cut, the locate ticket number and the backfill sign-off before shutting the machine down.
steps.title: Close out the excavation log
steps.why: The excavation log is what the next crew and the next inspection actually read — a cut that went cleanly but was never logged against its own ticket number leaves nothing behind to prove the locate was checked at all, which is the fact the whole job was resting on.
